title: Don't spoil it with reminders
hookLine: a kind word is better than charity followed by hurt (2:263–264)

lines: REMEMBER WHEN I DROVE THE TRUCK?
A GIFT TURNED INTO A DEBT.
cards: Remember when I drove the truck? Remember who paid for the pizza? A relative helped someone move years ago, and mentions it at every holiday since.

The help was real: a whole Saturday, a borrowed truck, a sore back. But somewhere around the tenth reminder, the help starts to feel like a bill, a debt that can never be paid off. Al-Baqarah knows this relative.

teach.b: Right after the seven ears of grain, the surah adds a condition. Verse two hundred sixty-two: those who spend and don't follow it with reminders of their generosity, or with hurt, their reward is with their Lord.

Verse two hundred sixty-three, in Pickthall's words: “A kind word with forgiveness is better than almsgiving followed by injury.” The Arabic for those reminders is mann: bringing up the favor, holding it over someone.
Verse two sixty-four pictures what mann does.
A smooth rock with a thin layer of soil on it. It looks like a field. Heavy rain falls and washes it bare.
Nothing grows: there was only stone underneath. The next verse paints the opposite.

A garden on high ground. Heavy rain falls, and it doubles its fruit; if no heavy rain comes, a light drizzle is enough. That's the gift given for God's sake, with no strings: it grows whatever the weather.
The tradition takes mann seriously. A hadith in Sahih Muslim names three people God will not speak to on the Day of Judgment, and one is al-mannan, the one who reminds people of what he gave.
And notice what the verse ranks above a spoiled gift: a kind word. Something gentle, with no money at all, is better than money with a sting.

how: Muslims are taught to give without reminding the recipient or expecting thanks; mann, recounting one's favors, is counted a serious fault, and many give quietly so as not to be tempted toward it.

o: holding a favor over someone by bringing it up
thanking someone again and again for a gift
a gift handed back to the giver later on

games.q: the rock and the garden — tap the pairs.
p: better than a gift with hurt

s: reminding someone of your gift can undo it
2:264 pictures it as rain washing soil off a rock.
the verse says any gift is better than a kind word
a kind word with forgiveness is better than a gift followed by injury.

games.q: you helped a friend through a hard month. now you're annoyed with them. what does al-Baqarah say about bringing it up?
games.why: don't follow a gift with reminders or hurt: it washes away like soil from a rock. a kind word is better.

practice: Think of a favor you've done for someone and kept score of since, out loud or in your head, and picture it as a stone you've been carrying.
Set it down by the road and walk on without looking back; if you pray, leave it with God, and if you don't, simply let it go.

wordCard.voice: Mann. Reminding someone of a favor, holding it over them — what al-Baqarah says washes a gift away like rain off a bare rock. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: reminding someone of a favor, holding it over them; one who does it is al-mannan.

carryVoice: Your line: give and forget. A kind word can be the whole gift. Day three hundred sixty, done.

sources.q: A kind word with forgiveness is better than almsgiving followed by injury.
